Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 98, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

(p-39) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surat al-Bayyina (The Clear Evidence)

Al-Alusi said: It is also called Surat al-Qiyama, Surat al-Balad, Surat al-Munfakkin, Surat al-Bariyya, and Surat Lam Yakun.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His Exalted saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists were not to be separated [from their disbelief] until there came to them clear evidence﴾ ﴿a Messenger from Allah, reciting purified pages﴾ ﴿within which are correct books﴾ ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after there had come to them clear evidence﴾.

Here He mentioned "those who disbelieved," then came "min" (from), and after it "the People of the Scripture and the polytheists." This indicates that the attribute of disbelief encompasses each of the People of the Scripture and the polytheists. It also indicates, once again, that the polytheists are not among the People of the Scripture, because of the presence of the conjunction (ʿataf), and that the People of the Scripture are not among the polytheists.

This question is well known among the theologians (mutakallimun) and the scholars of tafsir. They agreed that the People of the Scripture are the Jews and the Christians, that the polytheists are the worshippers of idols, and that disbelief (kufr) includes both groups.

"Ahl al-Kitab" is specific to the Jews and the Christians, but the disagreement is whether shirk (polytheism) also includes both of them.

Between the two groups there is a relation of general and specific: general in disbelief, and specific in that the People of the Scripture are the Jews and the Christians, and specific in that the polytheists are the worshippers of idols.

However, there are verses indicating that the designation of shirk also includes the People of the Scripture, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿And the Jews said, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their statement from their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded? They have taken their scholars and monks as lords other than Allah, and [also] the Messiah, the son of Mary. And they were not commanded except to worship one God; there is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ [At-Tawbah: 30–31].

(p-40) Thus He made the saying of each of the Jews and the Christians an act of shirk.

It is reported from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar that he prohibited marriage with a woman of the People of the Book, and said: "Is there any greater shirk than her saying: ﴿Allah has taken a son﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 116]?" Although he opposed the majority in prohibiting marriage with women of the People of the Book, he regarded them as polytheists.

Because of this difference and this possibility, the dispute arose regarding the designation of shirk: does it include the People of the Scripture or not? Yet we find a distinction in the Shariʿah in dealing with the People of the Scripture and dealing with the polytheists: it made lawful the slaughter of the People of the Scripture and did not make lawful the slaughter of the polytheists, and it made lawful marriage with women of the People of the Scripture and did not make it lawful with polytheist women, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 221].

And His saying: ﴿And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 10].

And He said: ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 10], clarifying the ruling regarding the women of the People of the Scripture. He said: ﴿And [lawful are] chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their due compensation﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 5]. Thus there is a difference in ruling between them.

Our father, the Shaykh Muhammad al-Amin, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, gathered these texts in removing the appearance of contradiction at His saying: ﴿And the Jews said, "Ezra is the son of Allah"﴾ mentioned earlier, in a detailed compilation whose substance is that the major shirk that expels one from the religion has types, and the People of the Scripture are characterized by some of them and not others, and so on to the end of what he presented, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him.

Perhaps in the very verse ﴿And the Jews said, "Ezra is the son of Allah"﴾ there is an allusion to what he mentioned, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, from two aspects:

The first: His saying: ﴿they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., they resemble them in their statement. This degree is characteristic of the polytheists in types of shirk.

The second: concluding the verse with the form of the present tense, "what they associate," whereas in Surat al-Bayyina He described the worshippers of idols by the noun "al-mushrikin."

(p-41) It is known that the form of the verb indicates renewal and occurrence, and the form of the noun indicates permanence and stability. So the polytheists of Makkah and others are constantly upon association and the worship of idols, while the People of the Scripture fall into it at times and at other times.

Some scholars held that disbelief is one religion, so they inherited from one another among all of them, while others prohibited that on the basis of difference, and knowledge is with Allah, Exalted.

* *

Note
The Magians remain, and the Sunnah has come that they are treated as the People of the Scripture, based on the hadith: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book."

As for His saying: ﴿not to be separated until there came to them clear evidence﴾, the interpretation of "munfakkin" has differed greatly among all the exegetes, to the point that al-Fakhr al-Razi, at the beginning of this surah, said verbatim: Al-Wahidi said in al-Basit: This verse is among the most difficult in the Great Qur'an in its composition and interpretation, and great scholars have stumbled over it.

Then he, may Allah have mercy on him, did not summarize how the difficulty arises.

I say the nature of the difficulty is this: the construction of the verse is: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists were not to be separated until there came to them clear evidence﴾, which is the Messenger ﷺ. Then he did not mention what they were not separated from, but it is known, since what is meant is the disbelief they were upon.

So the construction becomes: those who disbelieved were not to be separated from their disbelief until there came to them clear evidence, which is the Messenger. Then after that He said: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after there had come to them clear evidence﴾. This requires that their disbelief increased upon the coming of the Messenger, peace be upon him, so there appears to be a contradiction between the first verse and the second. This is the extent of the difficulty as far as I think. End quote, verbatim.

I have quoted his words to show the extent of the difficulty in the two verses, and it is based on the view that "munfakkin" means "abandoning," which is the view of all the exegetes.

What came from the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, in his dictation: that "munfakkin" means: (p-42) turning back from disbelief and misguidance, until there came to them clear evidence, i.e., it came to them.

However, in "munfakkin" there is an aspect that removes this difficulty, which is that "munfakkin" be taken in the sense of "left unattended" (matrukin), not in the sense of "abandoning" (tarikin). That is: they were not all left unattended in what they were upon of disbelief and polytheism until there came to them clear evidence, in the sense of His saying: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 36], and His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think that they will be left to say "We have believed" and they will not be tested?﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 1–2], i.e., they will not be left. Close to this is His saying: ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear evidence, and we will not leave our gods over your saying"﴾ [Hud: 53].

Abu Hayyan related a view from Ibn ʿAtiyyah, whose words are: "A third view, excellent in meaning, is possible concerning the meaning of the verse: that what is meant is that these people were not left unattended by the command of Allah, Exalted, His power and His regard for them, until Allah, Exalted, sends to them a warning Messenger, by whom the proof is established against them and by whom the blessing is completed upon those who believe. It is as if He said: they were not to be left neglected. There are parallels to this in the Book of Allah, Exalted." End quote.

So Ibn ʿAtiyyah's statement agrees with what we have mentioned, and removes the great difficulty for the exegetes, as we have previously stated.

Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, also had a statement on this, which we quote for its comprehensiveness; it is within his commentary on this surah in al-Majmuʿ, volume 61, page 594. He said:

Regarding the meaning of His saying, Exalted: "Those [who disbelieved] were not to be separated," there are three views mentioned by more than one exegete.

Is what is meant: they were not separated from disbelief?

Or: they were not those who denied Muhammad until he was sent, so they were not separated from Muhammad and from affirming his prophethood until he was sent.

Or: what is meant is that they were not left unattended until a messenger was sent to them.

He discussed these views and refuted them all, then said: So His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists were not to be separated﴾, i.e., they were not left to themselves by their own choice, doing whatever they desired, with no restraint upon them, just as the one who is "unfakk" (released) has no restraint upon him. He did not say "maftukin" (released), but said "munfakkin," and this is better... to his saying: The intended meaning is that they were not left unattended, not commanded, not forbidden, and no messengers were sent to them.

The meaning: Allah does not leave them free or abandon them; He does not release them until He sends to them a Messenger. This is like His saying: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾, not commanded and not forbidden. That is: does he suppose this will happen? This never happens at all; rather, he must be commanded and forbidden.

Close to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you might reason. And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and wise. Shall We then turn away the reminder from you [and disregard you] because you are a transgressing people?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 3–5]. This is a rhetorical question of denial, i.e., because of your transgression we would withhold sending down the reminder and turn away from sending messengers.

It becomes clear from all of this that the more correct sense of "munfakkin" is "left unattended," and by it the difficulty raised by al-Fakhr al-Razi disappears, the context is consistent, and the meaning becomes clear. And success is from Allah, Exalted.

His Exalted saying: ﴿until there came to them clear evidence﴾ ﴿a Messenger from Allah, reciting purified pages﴾.

He stated "clear evidence" in summary, then detailed it afterward: ﴿a Messenger from Allah, reciting pages﴾.

On this basis it has been said: the clear evidence is the Messenger himself in his person, because they knew him before his coming, as in His saying: ﴿And a messenger who comes after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [As-Saff: 6], and His saying: ﴿They recognize him as they recognize their own sons﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 146].

So his very existence ﷺ was a clear evidence for them.

For this reason it has come in authentic reports that they recognized him on the day of his birth by the appearance of the star of the prophet of circumcision, and so on to the end of his reports ﷺ. They used to seek victory through him over those who disbelieved. Likewise the polytheists knew him through the People of the Scripture, and by what he was characterized with ﷺ of excellent qualities, as Khadijah said to him at the beginning of revelation when he was frightened by it: "Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. By Allah, you join the ties of kinship, bear the burdens of others, help the poor, and aid in the calamities of time," and so on to its end.

And the saying of his uncle Abu Talib: "By Allah, I never saw him play with the children, nor did I know of him any lie," etc. They gave him the title al-Amin.

(p-44) And the incident of the splitting of his chest in his nursing; and it was also said of the story of his father ʿAbdullah, when a woman approached him wishing him for herself, and he refused. When he married and consummated with Aminah, the mother of the Prophet ﷺ, she met him after that and said to him: "I have no need for you." He said: "How did you use to approach me?" She said: "I saw a light in your face, so I wished that it would be mine. When you married and I placed it in Aminah, I no longer saw it in you, so I have no need for you."

All of these are indications that he ﷺ had in his person a clear evidence for them. Then Allah honored him with the message, so he was a Messenger reciting purified pages, free from falsehood, deviation, and whatever is unbefitting of the Qur'an.

Among what is cited as evidence for this is His saying concerning him: ﴿and as one who calls to Allah by His permission and as a light-giving lamp﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 46]. Accordingly, ﴿a Messenger from Allah﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "clear evidence," in the case of apposition; or the clear evidence is what the Messenger brings to them, of what he recites to them from the purified pages in which are correct books.

So the legislation contained in them and the information he proclaimed constitute the clear evidence. In any case, the clear evidence applies to all of them, just as it applies to the collection, and neither of the two is separated from the other: there is no Messenger except with a message that is recited, and no message recited except by a Messenger who recites it.

The term "al-bayyina" has been made definite to indicate the existence of a prior knowledge of it.

So it is as if it were said: "until there comes to them the clear proof described for them in their books." This is alluded to by what we mentioned earlier in the reports about 'Isa (peace be upon him) concerning it, and at the end of Surat al-Fath: ﴿That is their likeness in the Torah, and their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed that sends out its shoot﴾ [al-Fath: 29], and the rest of the verse.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 98, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Therein are books (kutub) of scripture﴾.

It is the plural of kitab (book). Al-Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, said in his dictation: "Kutub means maktubat (written things)."

Ibn Jarir said: "In the purified pages (suhuf, sheets of scripture) are books from Allah that are upright (qayyimah). It mentions the Qur'an with the best of mention and praises it with the best of praise."

Ibn Kathir reported this and limited himself to it.

Al-Qurtubi said: "The books mean the rulings (ahkam)," citing as evidence similar expressions such as ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] and ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21].

It was also said: "The upright books are the Qur'an, and it was called books because it includes sections (abwab) of clarification."

Al-Razi mentioned that it is possible that "books" means the verses written in the mushaf (the written codex), and this is close to the saying of al-Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him.

Al-Shawkani said: "What is meant is the verses and the rulings written in them. Although these meanings are correct, the apparent wording is more indicative that the meaning of books is included in it, in the sense of the writing of rulings."

What appears to be correct is that the indication of "books" is according to its apparent meaning, namely that those purified pages contain upright earlier books, as His saying, Exalted is He, makes explicit: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'la: 16-17], then He said: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former pages, the pages of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 18-19]. Similarly is His saying about the books of old in general: ﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 30], and His saying: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what is before it, and He revealed the Torah and the Gospel before this﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3-4].

Therefore He said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book know it to be sent down from your Lord in truth﴾ [al-An'am: 114], meaning: with what is in it of their upright books, whose revelation came earlier, as in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses and an example from those who passed away before you﴾ [al-Nur: 34].

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ﴾ [al-Naml: 76].

He also said: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming that which is before it﴾ [al-An'am: 92], and similar verses of this kind, which indicate that the verses of the Qur'an contain upright books that were revealed before. This has come in practice in the verse of al-Rahman. And His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein﴾, that is, in the Torah, ﴿that the life is for the life, the eye for the eye﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. These are among the upright books that the noble Qur'an included, as He said: ﴿And for you in retribution (qisas, legal retaliation) is life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179].

Perhaps this clarifies the meaning in what the exegetes narrated from Imam Ahmad, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "I have been commanded to recite to you Surat al-Bayyinah." He said: "And was I mentioned there?"

He wept, may Allah be pleased with him, because in it there is additional reassurance for him regarding his faith, that he believed in a Book that contained the upright earlier books. And Abdullah ibn Salam knew, concerning those books, that stoning was in the Torah, after its concealers had covered it, as is well known in the story. And Allah knows best.

The Qur'anic phrase: "And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after the clear evidence had come to them."

It is to be noted that the surah at its beginning speaks of the disbelievers in general, both from the People of the Scripture and the polytheists together. Here, however, the discourse concerns the People of the Scripture alone. This is specific to them in this context, to the exclusion of the polytheists, because they are the People of Scripture (ahl kitab), and they have knowledge of him (ﷺ) and of what he would bring. Allah says: "And previously they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved; but when there came to them that which they recognised, they disbelieved in it" [al-Baqarah: 89].

Likewise, in plain terms, is His saying: "And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves" [al-Shura: 14]. It is because of their knowledge of him before his coming, and their disagreement about him after his coming, that He singled them out here by mention in His saying: "And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after the clear evidence had come to them."

Note (tanbih)

Among the things that indicate the meaning we have mentioned of "scriptures upright" (kutub qayyimah) are two matters from the Book of Allah:

The first of them: the specification here of the People of the Scripture by the absence of the generality of the discourse concerning those who disbelieved, and the texts we have already presented.

The second: that when the Qur'an mentioned the Messenger reciting to the polytheists, He said: "It is He who raised among the unlettered (al-ummiyyin) a messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses" [al-Jumu'ah: 2]. This is the very same style, but He said "His verses" (āyātihi), because they had no knowledge of the other scriptures, so He limited it to the verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 98, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion, inclining toward Him﴾.

This does not necessitate division in his (ﷺ) command.

But here it has not specified the place of the command upon them to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion: is it in their earlier scriptures, or in this Qur'an that is recited to them in purified pages?

The Mighty Qur'an has clarified that this command exists in both their books and the Noble Qur'an. (p-47) From what is in their books is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah"﴾ [an-Nahl: 36].

And His saying: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion that which He enjoined upon Noah and that which We have revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham and Moses and Jesus: that you establish the religion and not be divided therein﴾ [ash-Shura: 13].

So establishing the religion and not being divided therein is the very same as worshipping Allah, sincere to Him in religion.

From what is in the Qur'an is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and fulfill My covenant [with you] that I will fulfill your covenant, and fear none but Me﴾ ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming that which is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it. And do not exchange My verses for a small price, and fear only Me﴾ ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth while you know [it]﴾ ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40–43].

Here He has explicitly stated the whole matter: that the upright scriptures mentioned in the purified pages are the books of the People of the Scripture, by His saying: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming that which is with you﴾, and that they were commanded in this Qur'an to establish prayer and give zakah, along with the same instructions mentioned, and establishing prayer is nothing but worshipping Allah with sincerity.

These commands, whether they are in their books or in the Qur'an, do not require division; rather they require unity and oneness.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾.

Al-qayyimah: a form (fa'ilah) from al-qawamah, and it is the utmost of uprightness.

It came after His saying: ﴿therein are upright scriptures﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 3], meaning: upright in its teachings.

He, may He be exalted, has explicitly stated that the Qur'an is the most upright and most just, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most suitable﴾ [al-Isra': 9], and He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has sent down upon His Servant the Book and has not made therein any deviance; [but has made it] upright﴾ [al-Kahf: 1–2]. So He negated deviance from it and affirmed uprightness for it.

This is the utmost in qawamah, as we have mentioned before, that the straight [path] may contain some curvature, like a paved road that is straight yet passes over elevations and depressions, and sometimes deviates to the right and left (p-48) despite its straightness. So with straightness it is not free of curvature.

But what is free of curvature and is affirmed as straight is the path that extends in a single direction without any deviation to either side, with straightness across its surface.

Thus is the Qur'an: it is the Straight Path. Therefore He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5], the upright religion, upright in itself and upright over other than it, and dominant over it. Like His saying: ﴿That is the upright religion﴾ [Yusuf: 40], and His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion, the way of Abraham, inclining toward truth; and he was not of those who associate others with Allah." Say, "Indeed, my prayer, my rites of sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds. No partner has He. And this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims"﴾ [al-An'am: 161–163].

Admonition

In this verse there is an explicit refutation of those who call, without knowledge, to a call that is not free of confusion, and that is not free of ambiguity: the call to the unity of religions. The point of confusion in it is that this statement contains truth and falsehood.

As for the truth, it is the unity of the roots, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion, inclining toward Him, and to establish prayer and give zakah﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5]. As for the falsehood, it is the vagueness that this leads to regarding the branches (furu'), together with the certainty among all that the branches of each religion may not all agree with the branches of the other religion. Thus prayer is not uniform across all religions, nor is fasting, and the like.

The Muslims have agreed that what counts is what the Qur'an details of the branches, and the Sunnah completes the detailing of what was stated in summary.

Here is the explicit text that this which the Qur'an brought is the upright religion, and that the Qur'an guides to that which is most suitable, where it is the superlative form, so it is impossible that anything else be equal to or equivalent to it, given the texts of the Qur'an, that Allah took the covenant from all the prophets: that if they reached Muhammad (ﷺ), they would surely believe in him, surely support him, and surely follow him, and He took the covenant from them regarding that. And the messengers informed their nations of that. Therefore there remains no room, at this time or any other, for a call of ignorance under a hollow banner, the unity of religions, but rather the Islamic religion alone: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19], ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]. (p-49) And success is from Allah, may He be exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 98, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding therein eternally. They are the worst of creatures.﴾

The word al-bariyyah (creation, creatures) has been recited with a hamza and with a yaa'. Naafi' and Ibn Dhakwan recited it with a hamza, while the rest recited it with a yaa'. Scholars differed regarding its derivation.

Al-Qurtubi said: al-Farra' said: If al-bariyyah is derived from al-baraa'ah with a fatha on the baa' and the raa', meaning dust (turab), then its root is non-hamzated, based on his saying: "barahu Allah yabruhu barwan," meaning He created him. It was also said: al-bariyyah derives from "bariitu al-qalam," meaning I shaped the pen.

This verse contains two issues. The first: that they are in the fire of Hell, abiding therein eternally. The discussion of the eternity of the disbelievers in the Fire has already been presented fully by the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us.

The second issue: that they are the worst of creatures. Al-bariyyah originally is al-bari'ah, the hamza was changed to a yaa' for ease, and the yaa' was assimilated into the baa'. Al-bari'ah means the creation, and Allah the Exalted is Bari' al-nasamah (the Creator of souls), He is the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner, glorified is He.

Among al-bariyyah are beasts and birds, and here the text is general in its scope, thus it conveys that those people are worse than animals and beasts.

The text has come explicitly to this meaning in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living beings in the sight of Allah are the deaf and dumb who do not reason﴾ [al-Anfal: 22]. He clarified that the intended ones are the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He has made them deaf and blinded their vision﴾ [Muhammad: 23], and He said about them: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind and those who are in manifest error?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 40]. So due to their deafness and blindness, they are in manifest error.

It is established that beasts are not in manifest error, because they know and affirm the Oneness of Allah, as came in the case of Solomon's hoopoe, which denounced to Bilqis and her people their prostration to the sun and the moon instead of Allah.

The text of Malik in the Muwatta' regarding the virtue of Friday: "There is no beast except that it pricks up its ears from the dawn of Friday until the rising of the sun, out of fear of the Hour." All of this is not available to the disbeliever in any part. Then in the Hereafter, when Allah gathers all the beasts and takes retribution for the hornless (animal) from the horned, He says to them: "Be dust." Then the disbeliever wishes that he had been like them, but it is not granted to him, as He said: ﴿On the Day when a man sees what his hands have sent forth, and the disbeliever says, "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [al-Naba': 40].

And Allah knows best: the beasts did not do good so as to remain to be rewarded for it, nor did they do evil so as to be punished for it, so they were neither for themselves nor against themselves, except what happened between them and each other. When retribution was taken for them from one another, their matter ended, and their end was their return to their origin, which is dust. Unlike the disbeliever, for upon him is the reckoning of obligations and the punishment of disobedience, so he is punished with eternal abiding in the Fire, and thus he is the worst of creatures.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 98, verse 7:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - they are the best of creation.﴾

The ruling here is general, like the ruling there, but here it concerns being the best and superiority (al-khayriyyah wa'l-tafdil).

As for the aspect of kind (min haythu al-jins), there is no difficulty, because the human being is the best of kinds: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾ [al-Isra: 70].

As for the aspect of generality (min haythu al-'umum), some scholars have said regarding it that there is something which indicates that the righteous among the believers are superior to the angels.

Perhaps what strengthens this inference is that some individuals of the human kind are superior to the generality of the individuals of the angelic kind, namely the Messenger (ﷺ). When some individuals of a kind are preferred, this does not preclude it for others of that kind. But is it the case that some individuals of this community after him are superior to the generality or to some individuals of the angels? This is the locus of the disagreement.

Al-Qurtubi has a discussion on this: its foundation is the root of the material (asl al-maddah) and the texts which come regarding the root of the material. If al-bariyyah is derived from al-bara, which is dust, then the angels do not enter under this preference; otherwise they do enter.

As for the texts, he said in the surah al-Baqarah, at His saying: ﴿He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33], the third issue: The scholars have differed in this matter as to which of them is superior, the angels or the children of Adam, upon two opinions. One view holds that the messengers from among humans are superior to the messengers from among the angels, and the saints from among humans are superior to the saints from among the angels.

(p-51) Others held that the Highest Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) is superior. Those who preferred the angels argued that they are honored servants who do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.

And His saying: ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. And His saying: ﴿Say, "I do not tell you that I have with me the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I tell you that I am an angel"﴾ [al-An'am: 50].

And by what is in al-Bukhari, that Allah says: "Whoever mentions Me in an assembly, I mention him in an assembly better than it," and this is a text that the Highest Assembly is better than the assembly of the earth.

Those who preferred the children of Adam argued by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - they are the best of creation﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 7], with the hamza, from bara'a Allah al-khalq (Allah created the creation), and by His saying (ﷺ): "Indeed the angels lower their wings for the seeker of knowledge, out of pleasure with him." Abu Dawud narrated it.

And because Allah boasts of the people of 'Arafat to the angels, and He does not boast except of the best. And Allah knows best.

Some scholars said: There is no way to be certain that the angels are better than them, because the way to that is the report of Allah, the report of His Messenger (ﷺ), or the consensus of the community.

And none of that is present here, contrary to the Qadariyyah and Qadi Abu Bakr, who said: The angels are superior. He said: As for those among our companions and the Shi'ah who said: The prophets are superior, because Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, and so on.

Then he refuted this inference.

We have brought up this discussion to explain the disagreement on this issue, which the word al-bariyyah includes. I believe that the preference is partial (juz'iyyah) and not total (kulliyyah), because the kind of mankind is other than the kind of the angels. Regarding the angels there is the text that they are: ﴿honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26], and regarding mankind there is the text ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾ [al-Isra: 70]. The difference between them is like the difference between the noun and the verb in indication.

For in the angels, with the noun, "honored" (mukramun), which indicates permanence and stability, while in the children of Adam, "We have honored" (karramna), which indicates renewal and occurrence.

And this is the reality: honor is established, binding, and continuous for the angels, unlike its case in the children of Adam, since in them (p-52) and in them, and it is not far-fetched to say that the preference in deeds is in terms of their issuing from the children of Adam and from the angels. The angels produce acts of goodness by nature or without any impulses of evil, unlike the children of Adam, whose acts of goodness issue from them with a double exertion, since the soul that blames (al-nafs al-lawwamah) and the soul that commands to evil (al-nafs al-ammarah bi'l-su') are both composed within them, along with similar matters from the animal side.

The double exertion is that he struggles against the factors of evil until he overcomes them, and exerts effort in doing good. He strives first to be freed from the impulses of evil, then he strives to carry out the doing of good. This is an exertion that calls for preference over an exertion from one side only.

The Sunnah has come with what witnesses to this, when he (ﷺ) mentioned to his companions regarding those who come after them that the one who acts among them has the reward of fifty. They said: "Fifty from us, or from them, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Rather, fifty from you, because you find helpers in goodness and they do not find them."

And the hadith: "A dirham outstripped a hundred thousand dirhams," and the Prophet (ﷺ) explained that the dirham outstripped the multiplied multiples, because it is only the second of two, while the hundred thousand is a part of a large total.

So the soul that gives away half of what it owns, and nothing remains for it except a dirham, is far better than one who spends a small portion of what it owns while a great amount of wealth remains for it. The factors and motives of giving in charge were different, implanted in the soul and opposed to each other. The dirham in its essence and quiddity is of the same kind as other dirhams; the quiddity and the kind did not vary, but the motives and factors for spending it varied. Perhaps the intended preference is of this type, and it is more appropriate. And Allah knows best.

The Qur'anic commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 98, verse 8:

Allah's words: ﴿Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual residence (jannat 'adn), beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever.﴾

In this verse there are four issues: three are general (mujmalah), whose explanation has come in the Qur'an, and the fourth is detailed (mufassalah), and it has supporting evidence.

As for the three general matters, the first is His words: ﴿Their reward with their Lord﴾. Reward (jaza') is in return for something that merits it, whereas "with their Lord" ('inda rabbihim) indicates that it is a bounty (tafaddul) from Him; otherwise He would have said, "Their reward from their Lord" ('ala rabbihim).

This is made clear by the explicit words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing is a place of success; gardens and grapevines; and maidens of equal age; and a full cup. They hear therein no ill speech or falsehood. A reward from your Lord, a gift accounted [sufficient]﴾ [al-Naba' 78:31–36]. Thus He stated explicitly that this entire reward is from their Lord, a gift (ata') to them from Him.

The second and third matters are His words: ﴿gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow﴾. He mentioned in general what is in the gardens and stated that rivers flow beneath them, while those rivers remain unspecified. The verse ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [al-Naba' 78:1] has detailed what has been prepared for them in Paradise: gardens, grapevines, maidens, drink, tranquility, and the absence of idle talk to the end of the passage. The detail of the rivers has also come in surah Muhammad, in His words: ﴿The likeness of Paradise which the God-fearing have been promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey. For them therein is every fruit and forgiveness from their Lord﴾ [Muhammad 47:15]. Abiding forever in this bliss is the completion of bliss.

* *

Allah's words: ﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him.﴾

This statement, concerning Allah's good pleasure (ridwan) upon the servants in Paradise, is considered to be of the type of the general after the specific (min bab al-'amm ba'd al-khass).

This has already been discussed in surah al-Layl, in His words: ﴿But the most righteous will avoid it, who gives his wealth to purify himself... and he is going to be satisfied﴾ [al-Layl 92:17–21]. They agreed that these verses refer to al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, as previously mentioned. In the following surah, al-Duha, His words came: ﴿And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha 93:5], meaning for the Messenger (ﷺ).

Here it is in general terms: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—those are the best of creation﴾. It is general for all believers who possess these attributes. Then He said: ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾. Evidence has also come that clarifies the cause of Allah's good pleasure upon them, which is due to their deeds, as in His words: ﴿Certainly was Allah pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾ [al-Fath 48:18]. Thus the pledge was the cause of the pleasure.

In this verse there is the report that Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him, but it does not specify the time of this pleasure: is it prior in this world or does it occur in Paradise? A verse has come that clarifies that it is prior in this world, namely His words: ﴿And the first forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers and those who followed them in excellence—Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:100]. Here His words "Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him" are followed by "and He has prepared for them gardens."

This is in the sense of a future promise, so the report of pleasure precedes it.

Likewise the verse of surah al-Fath concerning the pledge under the tree, where it says: ﴿Certainly was Allah pleased with the believers﴾ [al-Fath 48:18], is a report in the past tense, and it has been named "the Pledge of Ridwan" (bay'at al-ridwan).

Note (tanbih)

A question arises concerning this noble style: the servant truly needs to know Allah's pleasure upon him, since it is the ultimate of his hopes, as He said: ﴿That is the great achievement.﴾

As for the report of the servant's pleasure with Allah, is it the servant's right to be asked whether he is pleased with Allah or not? It is certainly not his right to be asked that. So the report of that is for its necessary benefit, which is that they are in the utmost happiness and contentment with what they have of bliss, to the point that they are pleased, and their contentment has surpassed the limit of bliss to the pleasure with the Bestower.

Something of this is also indicated by the last verse of surah al-Naba': ﴿a gift accounted [sufficient]﴾ [al-Naba' 78:36]. They said: they will be given until they say, "Enough for us, enough for us," that is, "sufficient for us."

* *

Allah's words: ﴿That is for whoever fears his Lord.﴾

The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) is directed at the whole of the reward mentioned above, and it has been mentioned that it is for those who believe and do righteous deeds. Here He says it is for whoever fears his Lord, which indicates that those deeds proceed from them out of desire (raghbah) and dread (rahbah): desire for what is with Allah, and dread of Allah. Similar to this is His words: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman 55:46], and His words: ﴿But as for one who feared the standing before his Lord and prevented the soul from desire, then indeed, Paradise will be the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:40–41].

The reality is that the attribute of fear of Allah the Exalted is the most comprehensive of all the attributes of goodness in a human being, because it is an attribute of the angels brought near, as Allah the Exalted said of them: ﴿They fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Nahl 16:50].

And the ruling has been generalized in that by His words: ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen—for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Mulk 67:12].

In this verse is the greatest secret, which is that the fear is in the absence from people, and this is the highest level of watchfulness (muraqabah) of Allah, and khashyah is the most intense fear.
